stories.headline: How do MLS' European-bred stars adjust to the playoffs? 'It's a challenge'
stories.summary: For MLS' biggest stars, they've spent their careers crowning champions based on the table. For them, adapting to the idea of the playoffs isn't easy.
stories.body:
After a stop-start, nine-month regular season, the MLS Cup playoffs are here, and for players, now is when the real work begins. The 34 games played between February and early November are a distant memory, useful for qualifying clubs for the postseason, but now is the competition that matters.

For European-bred stars joining the North American league, the playoffs are a curiosity, a novelty. After all, in the biggest domestic competitions across the Old World, the champion is the team that picks up the most points over the course of the campaign. So, in their new surrounds, does the regular season matter? How do players adjust to the postseason? Should teams focus solely on making a run to MLS Cup and disregard the Supporters' Shield?

All questions that don't have one single answer. Still, newcomers have their opinions. Former LA Galaxy superstar Zlatan Ibrahimovic called the system "s---" in 2019, while Inter Miami CF midfielder Rodrigo De Paul made headlines for saying that winning MLS Cup is harder than lifting the UEFA Champions League trophy.

MLS' current playoff format takes the top seven teams from each conference, while teams in eighth and ninth face off in a wild card match. The winners of the one-game play-in then complete the 16-team postseason field. Those 16 teams then contest the best-of-three Round 1 series, before the winners go on to the single-elimination conference semifinals, conference finals and MLS Cup.

"You play 34 games and then the real business starts," San Jose Earthquakes forward Timo Werner said to ESPN.

How big of an adjustment is the postseason?
The transition can be difficult for newcomers joining from a traditional football structure.

Goalkeeper Roman Bürki moved to St. Louis City in 2023 after a decorated career spent at Borussia Dortmund, SC Freiburg and four clubs in Switzerland. St. Louis made history by becoming the first expansion team to win their first four matches and conclude the regular season in first place of the Western Conference.

The team looked to be set up for success, but their playoff run told a different story. St. Louis fell to eighth-place Sporting Kansas City in just two matches in Round 1.

Frustration and shock filled the dressing room following the first loss. Players looked defeated even before traveling for the second match of the series.

"I remember being very, very tired in my head because it was my first time playing a whole year without a real break," Bürki told ESPN. "Back then, we played from January into November and so on. I just remember being mentally very tired.

"We were winning a lot and we had confidence and everything, and then towards the end of the season, like you could see the energy level was lower and lower and like it's just so hard for me to adapt to. I'm not new to playing a lot of games. In Europe we also played cup, played league games, we played in Champions League, but then at some point you had a break for at least three weeks. Something like this and just to keep going, it was very hard for me and hard to adjust."

Werner, who joined San Jose in January after playing in the Bundesliga and Premier League, was similarly concerned about exhaustion prior to his first ever MLS Cup playoffs.

"It's difficult because also at the end of the season, after a long year, you're tired," he said. "You think you are over the finish line, but no, we are not over the finish line. We still have the best to come, so it's a challenge. It is a challenge to be mentally focused on that, because knowing that the real deal is coming after the season, after the 34 games."

A less-important regular season?
Former Inter Miami defender Jordi Alba called the league's postseason "unfair" in 2024 after falling to Atlanta United in the first round after winning the Supporters' Shield and setting the record for most points in a single regular season.

Miami entered that postseason as the clear favorite with a star-studded roster, a historic 22W-8D-4L record and a three-game winning streak. But the league's ultimate glamor club fell in three games to Atlanta in a shocking upset.

"This format seems a little unfair to me," Alba said. "It is clear that it has been done this way for many years, but if you ask me, if it were up to me, I would have to be the champion of one conference against the champion of the other, to make it as fair as possible, that's how it is."

The format left Alba questioning whether the regular season even mattered.

MLS rewards the winner of the regular season with the Supporters' Shield and homefield advantage throughout the playoffs, but to most in and around the league, the Shield trails MLS Cup in importance, devaluing the effort of consistency throughout the season.

Ibrahimovic criticized the league's format for encouraging complacency during the regular season. After decades of playing for Europe's biggest clubs and sharpening a famously competitive attitude, the Swedish striker was appalled by a format he thought rewarded mediocrity.

"When you talk about the playoffs, we just need to make the playoffs, win the playoffs and that's it," Ibrahimovic said in 2019. "It doesn't matter if you lose or win [during regular season]. How can you learn mentality if you just need to learn the playoffs? I think the system is s--- ... Here you are in seventh place, you make the playoffs and you win. So, how do you create that mentality to be on your toes 24 hours a day? It's very difficult."

And now, since the number of clubs that qualify increased from six teams in each conference in 2018 to eight teams plus a play-in match in 2023, players feel an even lesser sense of urgency.

"It doesn't matter as much if you lose games in the regular season because the most important thing is making the playoffs, right?" Bürki said. "Seattle played like an average regular season [in 2024], but towards the end, they started to perform and make the playoffs and went to the first two rounds. And that's just the way you probably should approach the whole season.

"I wouldn't say it's meaningless, the regular season, but because you have that format, you don't necessarily need to get upset as much as when you don't win. In Europe, we have 34 games and that's it to win the trophy, and every game counts. Here, not every game counts the same way."

He isn't wrong. Seattle kicked off the 2024 campaign with just two wins in their first 11 matches before picking up momentum toward the end of the season and eventually reaching the Western Conference final.

The pattern continued in the first games of this year's Round 1. Supporters' Shield winners and new record points holders Nashville SC were upset by ninth-seeded FC Cincinnati, 1-0. Inter Miami, the No. 2 seed in the East, were dropped 3-0 by No. 7 seed Columbus.

Best-of-three frustrations
In a traditional two-legged tie, the scoreline in Miami would have conditioned the hosts to make every second count, but not in MLS. Instead, head coach Cristian Gonzalez took out Luis Suárez at halftime, replaced crucial midfielder Yannick Bright with recent academy signing Alex Shaw in the 62nd minute and substituted recently injured Fricio Caicedo for Telasco Segovia with more than 20 minutes left to be played.

With no aggregate score or goal difference to worry about, the Herons now enter Friday's Game 2 with a clean slate, know that the narrowest of wins will send the series to a decisive third game.

"You can lose the first game 5-0 and tie the next two games, win in PKs and you're going through? I don't like that," Seattle Sounders goalkeeper Stefan Frei said in 2024. Charlotte FC manager Dean Smith, who previously coached in the Premier League, criticized the league over the lack of impact a massive victory can have in the most crucial point of the season.

"I think if it's over too late and you win on goal differential, I think that should be it," he said in 2024. "The fact that you can go win 6-0 away and then draw at home and still not get through, it bothers me a little bit."

Sources told ESPN the best-of-three format will be eliminated in 2027, but for now teams must prepare for three potential first-round games.

The format may change over time but the playoffs will continue to be an integral part of MLS, whether its biggest European newcomers like it or not. It's up to players to find a way to adjust in order to reach the highest success in the North American league: MLS Cup.

stories.headline: 'Cole Palmer is the best No. 10 in the Premier League' - Tosin Adarabioyo
stories.summary: Tottenham's Tosin Adarabioyo has said that Cole Palmer is "the best No. 10 in the Premier League" and "one of the best players he has ever seen."
stories.body:
Tottenham's Tosin Adarabioyo has said that Cole Palmer is "the best No. 10 in the Premier League" and "one of the best players he has ever seen."

Palmer has faced criticism during a dip in form lately, with the attacker scoring just one goal and providing one assist in his last eight games for Chelsea, and was left out of Thomas Tuchel's England squad for the November internationals.

Tosin -- who was close friends with Palmer during his time at Chelsea -- jumped to the defence of his former teammate.

"Of course, I am surprised [he was left out of the last England squad]," Tosin said as reported by The Athletic. "For me, he is the best No. 10 in the Premier League."

When asked why Tuchel had left Palmer out of the squad, the German said "he misses too many opportunities to impress."

"No one can chat s--- about Cole," Tosin added. "For me, he's one of the best players I have ever seen.

Chelsea have one win in their last four league games, the latest sobering result a 4-1 thrashing at the hands of Leeds United, who claimed their first victory at Stamford Bridge since 1999.

stories.headline: Qatar Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 heads to Qatar for the second leg of its final triple header of the 2026 season.
stories.body:
Formula 1 heads to Qatar for the second leg of its final triple header of the 2026 season.

Max Verstappen fended off his rivals to take a stunning victory under the lights at the Las Vegas Grand Prix last time out.

McLaren's Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri took the final spots on the podium.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 22nd round.

- Max Verstappen mocks George Russell in brutal outburst: 'So far below my level'

- Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc 'unmanageable' - Ferrari boss

- Max Verstappen, George Russell's latest war of words unlikely to stay in Vegas

Qatar Grand Prix schedule
All times in GMT

Friday, November 27

Practice One: 1.30 p.m. - 2.30 p.m.

Practice Two: 5 p.m. - 6 p.m.

Saturday, November 28

Final Practice: 2.30 p.m. - 3.30 p.m.

Qualifying: 6 p.m. - 7 p.m.

Sunday, November 29

Qatar Grand Prix: 4 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Qatar Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Lusail Circuit

The Qatar Grand Prix takes place under the floodlights at the Lusail Circuit. It is one of the most demanding on the calendar with long straights and sweeping high-speed corners coupled with intense heat and humidity, making conditions for the cars and drivers difficult.

It was originally built as a motorbike circuit before it joined the F1 calendar in 2021 on a 10-year contract. Qatar did not host a race in 2022 as they focused on the FIFA World Cup.

Qatar Grand Prix

Circuit: Lusail International Circuit; Lusail, Qatar

Previous winners in Qatar

2021: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2023: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2025: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2021

Laps: 57 laps of 5.4km

Lap record: 1:22.384, Lando Norris (2024)

Most wins: Verstappen (2023, 2024 and 2025). Lewis Hamilton (2021) is the only other winner.

Most poles: Hamilton (2021), Verstappen (2023), George Russell (2024) and Piastri (2025) have each taken pole.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Qatar Grand Prix is forecast to be sunny with a gentle breeze across the weekend. It's a night race so conditions are dry with highs of 24°C on Sunday.

What happened last time out?

McLaren's Piastri pipped teammate Norris to pole position as the battle for the world title continued with two races remaining.

During the race, Red Bull's Verstappen benefited from a McLaren strategy error to win his seventh race of the season, taking the three-way title race to the season finale in Abu Dhabi.

Piastri was leading the race and Norris was running in third, but the Papaya team decided against pitting under the Safety Car. Piastri ended the race in second, with Norris in fourth.

Who will win this year?

Verstappen looked unstoppable in Las Vegas and will be targeting his fifth win of the season in Qatar.

Mercedes' Russell was well in the mix last time out but will be looking to respond after Verstappen said the Englishman was "so far below his level" as their feud intensified.

Both teams look strong, so the rivalry could well continue in Qatar. Drivers up and down the grid will also be limited to 27 laps on each set of tyres, which will play massively into teams' strategies.

Tensions between Ferrari teammates Hamilton and Charles Leclerc continue to heat up after boss Fred Vasseur labelled them "unmanageable."

Don't count out new world champion Kimi Antonelli who is always one to watch after an impressive season.

stories.headline: Rashee Rice, Chiefs believe he caught pivotal 3rd-down pass late vs. Bills
stories.summary: WR Rashee Rice -- along with several members of the Chiefs -- felt he caught the ball on a pivotal third-down pass with less than two minutes left at the Bills.
stories.body:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- In the box score of Thursday's game, a primetime showdown where the Kansas City Chiefs fell to the Buffalo Bills 13-10, the last time receiver Rashee Rice touched the ball was when he dropped a pass.

However, Rice -- along with several members of the Chiefs -- felt he caught the ball on a pivotal third-down pass with less than two minutes left, a play that could've ignited a potential game-winning drive.

"Yes, I did," Rice said with a blank expression when asked if he believed he made the reception.

Instead, Rice said none of the officials explained to him why his 11-yard catch on third-and-10 from the Chiefs' 9-yard line was overturned into an incompletion after a replay review was conducted by the NFL's headquarters in New York City. The play ended with Rice attempting to make a contented catch in the middle of the field after he was hit, while in the air, by Bills safety Amani Hooker.

A few minutes later, the Bills and their fans inside Highmark Stadium cheered when referee Alex Kemp announced that the pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes was incomplete because the ball, while in Rice's right hand, hit the turf.

"We were first told that they were reviewing the spot, so I didn't even know that we were reviewing the catch," Mahomes said. "From my angle, when I threw the ball, I thought his hand was under the ball."

Mark Butterworth, the NFL's vice president of instant replay, explained the league's ruling after the game in a pool report.

"As the receiver [was] going to the ground, he had the ball in his right hand and when he contacted the ground, his hand slid up the ball and we deemed that a loss of control," Butterworth said. "The hand moving up the ball is what we deemed the loss of control."

Chiefs coach Andy Reid disagreed with the league's assessment.

"I'm not quite sure what they saw," Reid said. "I saw he had control of the ball and his elbow hit and then the ball hit [the turf] but he had control. Normally in those situations, it's got to be clear and obvious. To me, that was not clear and obvious."

Two players who discussed the play while the review was being shown inside the stadium were Chiefs center Creed Humphrey and defensive lineman Ed Oliver. Of course, they disagreed on what the result of the play should've been.

"He was all excited, like, 'Yeah, they caught it,'" Oliver said of Humphrey. "I watched it back and I was, like, 'Aw s---, he dropped it.' He was like, 'No way.' I was like, 'Yeah [Rice] did.' [Humphrey] was still in disbelief. But I knew. [As] soon as I [saw] the ball hit the ground, I knew it. That just [gave the] defense a boost of energy, a boost of life, getting off the field."

Even though the Chiefs punted the ball to the Bills following the review, they regained possession 90 seconds later. With just 26 seconds remaining, the Chiefs' final drive was doomed when Mahomes, from shotgun, dropped the snap from Humphrey, which led to a five-yard loss.

The Chiefs were forced to punt again when Mahomes' intermediate pass to tight end Travis Kelce on third-and-10 went incomplete. Those poor plays deep in their own territory led to the Chiefs giving the ball back to the Bills, who won the game on a 57-yard field goal from kicker Tyler Bass as time expired.

"When you're in the conditions you're in, you have to be locked in the entire time," Mahomes said of the wet, cold and windy weather. "I've got to be better there, catching that snap at the end of the game. It didn't give us a chance to get anything going, which ended up causing us to lose on the field goal.

"I know I'm trying to look at the defense, but, at the same time, you have to start with getting the snap the right way. That's just stuff that can't happen in a game like this."

One major advantage the Bills (10-1) had over the Chiefs (8-3) for much of the was the field position battle. Entering the game, the Chiefs ranked 30th in special teams, per ESPN's FPI. Thursday's game was the worst that the unit, under Dave Toub, the longtime special teams coordinator, has been this season. Punter Matt Araiza shanked several punts and even dropped the ball before attempting a punt. Araiza's final punt, which was partially blocked, was returned to the 39-yard line, setting up the Bills' game-winning field goal.

"Field position was a big thing," Reid said of the special teams unit. "We've got to do better. But the leadership [under Toub], I feel comfortable with."

With six minutes left, kicker Harrison Butker attempted a 46-yard field goal, one that would've given the Chiefs a three-point lead. But Butker continued his struggles this season, missing the kick wide right.

Butker is tied with Green Bay Packers kicker Trey Smack for the most missed kicks this season with nine -- eight field goal attempts and one extra point attempt. Since the start of the 2024 season, Butker's 24 missed kicks -- 17 field goal attempts and seven extra point attempts -- are the most in the NFL.

"You obviously want to do what you can to help the team, and I didn't do that," Butker said. "It's a tough loss. I'm not happy with the result and I'm not happy with [my] performance. Again, it's the same miss, off to the right. I can't explain it. I'm missing a lot of kicks."

ESPN Bills reporter Nick Suss contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Devils defenseman Brenden Dillon suspended 4 games for illegal hit to the head
stories.summary: Devils defenseman Brenden Dillon has been suspended for four games for an illegal hit to the head of Blue Jackets defenseman Denton Mateychuk.
stories.body:
New Jersey Devils defenseman Brenden Dillon received a four-game suspension Thursday for an illegal hit to the head of Columbus Blue Jackets defenseman Denton Mateychuk.

Dillon was assessed a match penalty for the check during the first period of the Devils' 3-2 shootout win in Columbus on Wednesday night. Mateychuk left the game after the hit.

Dillon forfeits $82,474.24 based on his average annual salary and under the terms of the collective bargaining agreement. The money goes to the Players' Emergency Assistance Fund.

On the play, Mateychuk skated through neutral ice and entered the zone before moving the puck to a teammate. Once the puck was gone, Dillon finished a "high, hard check, elevating upward and unnecessarily and making Mateychuk's head the main point of contact on a hit where such head contact was avoidable," the NHL's department of player safety said in a video.

Blue Jackets coach Rick Bowness said after the game: "I've coached Dillon. He's not a dirty player. He's a hard player. He caught him in a bad spot, and that's a bad hit. It is."

Bowness said Wednesday that he spoke with Mateychuk and the defenseman "feels fine." Bowness added that "protocol will take over and we'll go from there."

stories.headline: Friday Night Lights,' 'Ted Lasso' top poll ranking 21st-century sports shows
stories.summary: A Seton Hall poll crowns America's favorite modern fictional sports TV series.﻿
stories.body:
It's been quite the year for scripted sports series, with milestones worth celebrating and new chapters worthy of clearing space on the couch.

"Friday Night Lights" hit its two-decade anniversary. "One Tree Hill" turned 23 -- a number Nathan Scott and Michael Jordan would both approve of. On the more modern side, "Ted Lasso" returned for its fourth season, while "All American" wrapped up its Season 8 series finale.

Through different eras and sports, fans have plenty of reasons to get invested, so we tapped Seton Hall for a poll on America's favorite sports show of the 21st century.

"Friday Night Lights" and "Ted Lasso" took the top spots among the general population at 16% and 15%, respectively. The Texas-based football drama also held the edge among avid sports fans, 25% to 22%, and casual sports fans, 23% to 18%.

"The two leaders in the clubhouse for top series indicate that depth and consistency resonate the most with all sports fans," said Len DeLuca, associate director, Seton Hall Sports Poll and instructor in the Seton Hall Stillman Center for sport management. "'Friday Night Lights' was on NBC 14 years before 'Ted Lasso' premiered on Apple TV. This proves that sports content is agnostic to platform."

Whether your loyalty lies with the Dillon Panthers, the Tree Hill Ravens or AFC Richmond, there's a good chance your favorite fictional team has put you through highs and lows. And much like rooting for a real team, picking a favorite show can inspire a spirited debate.

Here are the key findings.

Football leads a multisport lineup
Among the general population, "Friday Night Lights" led all shows at 16%, with "All American" at 10%, "The Game" at 8% and "Ballers" at 7%. That gave football four of the eight highest-polling series overall. Viewers had plenty of interest in the drama surrounding the game, from high school rivalries to the business of professional sports.

Still, football didn't sweep the podium: Soccer's "Ted Lasso" and karate's "Cobra Kai" finished second and third at 15% and 13%, respectively. With 12%, "A League of Their Own" added representation for baseball and took the fourth spot. Hockey's "The Mighty Ducks: Game Changers" and basketball's "One Tree Hill" also drew 7% each, matching "Ballers."

The generation gap
The age ranges didn't differ entirely, but different generations tended to root for different fictional teams.

18-34: "Ted Lasso" led with 17%, followed by "All American," "The Game" and "The English Game" at 14% each. Newer titles also found an audience here: "Heated Rivalry" drew 10%, its strongest showing across the age groups.

35-54: This group showed the most love for "Cobra Kai," which topped its list at 19%. "Friday Night Lights" followed at 18%, with "Ted Lasso" at 15%. "One Tree Hill" and "Eastbound & Down" also had their strongest showings here at 10% each.

55+: "Friday Night Lights" took the lead at 17%, narrowly ahead of "A League of Their Own" at 16%. "Ted Lasso" rounded out the top three at 13%. The drop-off was sharper for teen dramas such as "All American" and "One Tree Hill," which drew 5% and 3%, respectively.

Commonalities and contrasts between sports fans and nonfans
Sports fans and nonfans found some common ground, even if they weren't watching the same shows. "Friday Night Lights" led among sports fans at 23%, followed by "Ted Lasso" at 19% and "Cobra Kai" and "A League of Their Own" at 16% each.

Among nonfans, "Cobra Kai" moved into first at 8%, with "Ted Lasso" and "A League of Their Own" tied at 7%. Coach Eric Taylor (played by Kyle Chandler) had a tougher time with that crowd, as "Friday Night Lights" drew 5%.

The biggest divide, though, was in those who selected "don't know/no opinion": 69% of nonfans compared with 28% of sports fans. The crossover appeal is there, but viewers with less interest in sports need more motivation to tune in.

The men's and women's lineups look a little different
"Friday Night Lights" and "Ted Lasso" finished first and second among both men and women, but the order differs after that. Among men, "Cobra Kai" took third at 15%, followed by "A League of Their Own" at 11%.

Women flipped those two, with "A League of Their Own" drawing 14% and "Cobra Kai" at 11%. "Make It or Break It" and "Heated Rivalry" also drew higher percentages among women than men, both at 6% to 4%.

New shows are earning their stripes
Some newer series are already finding a place alongside the familiar favorites. "Chad Powers" drew 6% overall, followed by "Heated Rivalry" at 5% and "Running Point" and "Off Campus" at 4% each.

For avid sports fans, "Chad Powers" reached 13%, matching "The Game" in that group. "Heated Rivalry," meanwhile, had its strongest showing among adults ages 18-34 at 10%. The established shows have a head start, but the newcomers are getting some playing time.

Editor's Note: These results are derived from a Seton Hall Sports Poll conducted Oct. 8 to Oct. 13, 2026, among 1,632 adults. The Poll, which is sponsored by The Sharkey Institute within Seton Hall University's Stillman School of Business, features a national representative sample from YouGov Plc., weighted on U.S. Census Bureau figures for age, gender, ethnicity, education, income and geography with a margin of error of +/- 3.0 percent.

stories.headline: Sparks forward Cameron Brink, Ben Felter wed at Stanford
stories.summary: The couple met in 2021 and was engaged in 2024 before marrying at their alma mater's Memorial Church.
stories.body:
Cameron Brink and Ben Felter have officially tied the knot after holding a ceremony on Nov. 14 at their alma mater Stanford's Memorial Church.

According to a report Tuesday from Vogue Magazine, which shared behind-the-scenes details and images, the Los Angeles Sparks forward had four bridal looks, including a custom dress from bridal designer Danielle Frankel for the ceremony, and another for the reception.

Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry and his wife, Ayesha, were among those in attendance. Curry and Brink are godsiblings as their fathers were teammates at Virginia Tech, and their mothers were roommates on campus.

The reception was at Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay, while vows were exchanged at Memorial Church, one of the earliest interdenominational churches in the West. The waiting list to get married there can be up to four years, but alumni receive a shorter period, according to Vogue. The couple told the magazine that they always knew they wanted to wed there.

"Walking past the ornate mosaics on my way to class was always the best part of my day," Brink said.

Brink and Felter met at Stanford in the fall of 2020. The two began dating in March 2021 after Felter sent Brink an email in which he included his phone number. Felter, who rowed at Stanford, proposed to Brink in Paris in September 2024.

The No. 2 pick in the 2024 WNBA draft, Brink averaged a career-high 9.5 points plus five rebounds and 1.8 blocks for Los Angeles in the 2026 season.

stories.headline: Navajo Stirling belts another former champ, moves up in rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
If you've ever worn a UFC light heavyweight championship belt, watch out for Navajo Stirling.

His two most recent victories have come against former 205-pound champions, both knockouts. After a first-round finish of Jan Blachowicz in August, the New Zealander knocked out Jiří Procházka in Saturday's UFC Fight Night main event in Qatar.

As a result, Stirling leapfrogs Procházka in the ESPN divisional rankings, rising to No. 3 at light heavyweight. After his fourth straight knockout overall, Stirling (12-0) is right behind the division's champion, Carlos Ulberg, Stirling's training partner at City Kickboxing in Auckland. The No. 1 ranking belongs to former champion Magomed Ankalaev, who called out Stirling after Saturday's fight.

The weekend's UFC fights also led to changes in the featherweight and men's flyweight top 10s. Aljamain Sterling lost a 145-pound fight to Kevin Vallejos and drops four spots to No. 7, right below Vallejos. stories.headline: Price tag for Tassie's new AFL stadium goes up, again
stories.summary: The estimated cost of a new 23,000-seat waterfront venue, set to eventually become the home of the Tasmania Devils, has risen again.
stories.body:
Tasmania's new AFL stadium has suffered another cost blowout, causing the premier to break a promise to cap the state's spend as critics fear the end price will be far higher.

The cost estimate for the 23,000-seat roofed venue at Macquarie Point in Hobart has increased from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion.

On top of the figure is $132 million for broader precinct infrastructure, project delivery costs of $183 million and unspecified contingencies, taking the total to $1.54 billion.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff previously pledged to cap Tasmania's contribution to the build at $875 million as part of a deal to get the project through parliament.

But he conceded on Tuesday the state would have to cover the slated $100 million increase via extra borrowings.

"The previous cost estimate, which we announced ... some 14 months ago, there's been a lot of water under the bridge since that point," Mr Rockliff said.

The premier confirmed the project wouldn't head back to parliament for the approval of the necessary extra funding, despite previous assurances it would.

The latest estimate reflects increases in the cost of construction, sustained high oil and materials prices, higher labour costs and its complexity, the state government said.

The stadium is expected to be ready for the 2031 AFL season and was a condition of the Tasmania Devils being granted a licence to enter into the national competition in 2028.

It initially had a price tag of $715 million.

Mr Rockliff said the state had reached out to the federal government and AFL for extra money on top of their $240 million and $15 million contributions.

Anti-stadium group Our Place Hobart said the new cost estimate failed to take into account other factors, including the interest bill and the exact cost of contingencies.

Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff described the ongoing cost increases as a deep betrayal of Tasmanians.

"Who knows where the final price for the stadium will end up?" she said.

"What we do know is there's been now a fifth major cost blowout and there's not yet a contract price locked in for this massive project."

Federal independent MP Andrew Wilkie fears the stadium will end up costing $2 billion.

"Once you add the cost of the debt over a decade, the total cost to the Tasmanian taxpayer is closer to $3.5 billion," he said.

Devils chief executive Brendon Gale said the question of any additional funding from the AFL was a matter for the sport's governing body.

"The politicians can politic. We'll get on with building our club," he said.

"People have their views and are entitled to them. But based on my experience, people never look back. These types of projects transform cities and states."

The release of updated costs came ahead of schedule after the government bowed to political pressure to make the figures public before the end of the parliamentary year.

In mid-October, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder. A final contract is set to be signed by the end of 2026.

BESIX Watpac recently built a 30,000-seat roofed stadium in Christchurch in New Zealand which cost about $540 million.

Mr Rockliff said the final contract price for the Hobart stadium was unlikely to differ from the $1.23 billion estimate.

The stadium has been deeply divisive in Tasmania amid rising state debt, a stretched health system and other under-pressure services.

The AFL and federal government have been contacted for comment.

stories.headline: 'Can't judge them': who Papenhuyzen wants at the Storm
stories.summary: Ex-Melbourne star Ryan Papenhuyzen has made some big calls on who should be the next Storm coach and the one to keep from Cameron Munster and Harry Grant.
stories.body:
Ryan Papenhuyzen empathises with Cameron Munster but believes Melbourne must prioritise keeping Harry Grant if the NRL powerhouse can't hold on to both superstars.

Munster on Tuesday rejected an offer from the Storm believed to be for one year with the option of another season, labelling the terms "disappointing".

The Storm are also fighting to keep Grant, and Papenhuyzen was unequivocal when asked on Wednesday who the club should target if salary-cap pressures meant only one of the newly crowned Australian World Cup winners could stay.

"I went through something similar as Munster where I thought the club had low-balled me," the happily retired 2020 premiership-winning hero told AAP.

"But having my time out of the game now, they've got their reasons for offering those certain amounts and it might not be enough (for Munster).

"Penrith have done it for years and years. They get to a point where they can't hold their players and they've got a price for their players.

"So I understand Munster's perspective. He wants to earn as much as he can in his career and he wants to win a premiership, so that probably limits his opportunities.

"If a club's got money and they're in a premiership window, it's probably a good chance he'll go to that club."

At 28, skipper Grant is four years younger than Munster and more important long-term to the Storm, Papenhuyzen believes.

"Harry's done a brilliant job in terms of leadership," the ex-Clive Churchill Medallist turned caddy said after playing in the Australian PGA Championship pro-am in Sydney.

"The amount of care he has for everyone in that group and the way he thinks about the game, I feel really sorry for him over the last 12 months (when Melbourne missed the finals) because he's always trying to find new ideas to bring everyone.

"He's a great leader for that club going forward. I'd hate to see him go because he's a player you want to build a club around and I guess Munster is towards the back end of his career.

"He had a great World Cup, but World Cups are different to NRL seasons. You've got to lock in for a month with that, and an NRL season's a long time."

Pressed on who he'd keep as a priority, Papenhuyzen said: "Harry's probably the one leadership-wise. Just his qualities are really admirable.

"You know what Munster brings to the game. He gives you confidence standing next to him, knowing what he's going do, but I just think Harry ..."

With coach Craig Bellamy confirming he is moving on at the end of 2027, Papenhuyzen also suspects Grant might be a better for the Storm's new mentor, whomever that may be.

"Harry's really respected and in terms of trying to keep the culture, he's very open-minded too," the BMW golf correspondent said.

"He's open to new ideas, whereas Munster is very much like Bellamy - he's sort of got his way and it's worked for him for so long.

"Whatever they both decide to do, you can't judge them. It's never a right or wrong decision."

Papenhuyzen believes it would be "awesome" if Billy Slater succeeded Bellamy, but suspects "life is too good" for the Storm legend to be a head NRL coach.

"I love Jyles. If he went back there, I'd be awfully encouraged of how well they're going to go. They'd probably be my two."

But Papenhuyzen, also open to helping out the new coach, nominated Bellamy's son Aaron as a left-field option.

"Aaron's awesome with people," he said.

"He's awesome with the wider playing group and he understands that Craig sometimes pushes the boundaries. Aaron's a bit more like Wendy - Craig's, Craig's wife.

"They're both a bit more more gentle, so you've got that loving, nurturing side and potentially (he could do the job).

"I do know you just need people around you. We'd be silly to say the coach controls everything."

stories.headline: Source: MLS owners agree new 16-team playoff format starting in 2027-28
stories.summary: MLS team owners have agreed on a new playoff format for the 2027-28 season featuring 16 teams, a source confirmed to ESPN.
stories.body:
Major League Soccer's team owners have agreed on a new playoff format for the 2027-28 season, one that will feature 16 teams with two rounds of home-and-home series and single elimination thereafter, a source with knowledge of the league's plans confirmed to ESPN.

The format was approved by team owners at the MLS Board of Governors meeting in Miami on Nov. 12. Aggregate goals will be used to determine the winners in the first two rounds with extra time and penalties used to break ties, though that approach could change, the source said.

The new approach to the postseason will be implemented in conjunction with the league's shift to a summer-to-spring calendar that more closely aligns with leagues in Europe.

The calendar transition will feature what is being called a "sprint season" to take place in the first half of 2027. That competition will feature a 14-game regular season, with the top eight teams from each conference qualifying for the playoffs. Each playoff round in that competition will be single elimination, culminating in MLS Cup on Memorial Day weekend.

The Athletic was the first to report the new playoff format. An official announcement is expected on Dec. 3. The source added that the new format was discussed with broadcast partners and sponsors.

The agreed-upon format for the 2027-28 season reflects a more simplified approach than what was previously being considered.

That previous format would have featured 20 teams in a double elimination system inspired by Australian Rules Football. The number of qualifiers received pushback from fans and media, with the league ultimately agreeing to scale back the number of teams reaching the postseason.

MLS has frequently modified its playoff format over the course of its existence, oscillating between best-of-three and home-and-home series, as well as whether away goals counted as a tiebreaker.

Currently the league uses a system in which 18 teams reach the postseason. A preliminary wild card round involving four teams feeds into a 16-team setup featuring a best-of-three series in the conference quarterfinal round. The conference semifinal, conference final and MLS Cup final are all single elimination.

Part of what drove consideration for the Aussie Rules format was increasing the inventory of playoff games, which typically draw the best ratings. The new format will still contain a total of 27 playoff games. The current approach features between 25 and 33 games. Reducing the number of playoff teams from 18 to 16 will also place more emphasis on the regular season.

The source also confirmed that the 2027-28 regular season will feature a revised format. Teams will be split among five divisions, and will play each of their division rivals twice, and the remainder of the teams in the league once for a total of 34 games.

While the final details still need to be approved, the league is looking at playoff qualification being determined partly by how a team finishes in its division, as well as a league-wide table. Five of the games against division rivals will take place at the end of the season to add some drama to the fight for playoffs places.

stories.headline: Would any USMNT players really make Man United better if they followed Poch?
stories.summary: Now that USMNT manager Mauricio Pochettino has taken over Man United, would it make sense for USMNT players to join their ex-coach?
stories.body:
If you follow the U.S. men's national team, here's a good sanity check: Imagine going back in time -- say, 15 years -- and telling your past self about the current situation.

"Yeah, so there's this guy who came up through the FC Dallas academy, moved to Schalke when he was a kid, started for them as an 18-year-old when they finished second in the Bundesliga behind Bayern Munich, and then moved to Juventus. He has played more Serie A matches for Juve than anyone else in the seven seasons since he joined the team."

"And he just did this news conference where he said, 'Guys from here being talked about going to Manchester United' was 'inevitable.' Oh, and this is important: he was saying that because Manchester United just poached the USMNT manager in the middle of the Premier League season."

Think about all the assumptions your 15-years-younger self would be making, whenever they had regained consciousness after suffering the double-whammy of learning that time travel exists and that the USMNT was one step below Manchester United in the global pecking order.

... Schalke are one of the best development clubs in the world, and Juventus are one of the best clubs in the world, so one of the best soccer players in the world plays for the USMNT now? And then, well, the USMNT coach is now coaching Manchester United, which might be the best club in the world. If my math is right, then there was a World Cup a couple of months ago -- in summer 2026 -- so ... wait ... did the U.S. just win the World Cup?

At this point, you'd disappear back to the present, allowing yourself to dream of a more hopeful future -- rather than explaining what happened to the Italian economy in the aughts, or what went down at Manchester United after Sir Alex Ferguson left, or what the USMNT's score against Belgium was.

But even with the relative changes in station over the past decade-plus, it's still a surreal thing to say today: Manchester United just hired away the USMNT manager. And, as Weston McKennie suggested, this always happens: Transfer rumors connect the manager of a new club with a smattering of players from the manager's old team.

All of which brings us here: Would any of Mauricio Pochettino's former players actually make Manchester United better? And even if they would, should United sign any of them?

What do Manchester United need?

There are three clear, interrelated issues with the way United's team plays and the way United's team was built.

The first: They're old. In fact, they're as old as Arsenal.

Now, you might be saying, "But Arsenal are the best team in the league!" But, well, Arsenal are the best team in the league, in part, because they're old. After multiple seasons of signing exclusively young players, they've spent the past two years adding established players who are late in their prime to the roster. They are trying to win as much as possible right now, and so their average age, weighted by minutes played, is 27.2 -- tied for third oldest in the league.

Although they finished third last season, United were clearly not a title contender coming into the Premier League season -- and, well, they're currently in 19th place. After Sunday's embarrassing loss to Liverpool, prediction markets now give them a 19% chance of being relegated. Once again, this team should be building for future title contention -- not contention to win right now.

Perhaps connected to that is the team's inability or unwillingness to press. The stats app Futi measures team's tendencies across a variety of stylistic markers. One of which is: "Stay compact to deny space or press to win the ball during the opponent's buildup?" Here's where United landed on that spectrum before Pochettino took over:

It's even worse when you look at what they do soon after possession is turned over: "Press aggressively to win back lost balls or fall back to recover defensive structure?"

While the league has moved toward a much more aggressive stance in these situations, United have gone in the opposite direction:

And it hasn't helped the defense in any way.

Only one team has conceded more expected goals than United this season:

We know that Pochettino wants his teams to press, and we know that pressing tends to favor younger, more energetic, and more mobile players. We also know that Pochettino's USMNT ticked both of these boxes at the World Cup: They were one of the more aggressive pressing teams in the tournament, and -- despite the presence of 39-year-old Tim Ream -- the ninth-youngest team in the field, weighted by minutes played.

Would any USMNT players make Man United better?

Given everything we've just gone over -- or, you know, what you might've watched Sunday -- the obvious place to start is in the back.

Man United goalkeeper Senne Lammens is young and roughly a league-average Premier League starter, and goalkeeper might be the weakest position in the USMNT pool. No Americans would be an upgrade here.

At the back, United's four most-used players this season are Diogo Dalot at right back, Luke Shaw at left back, and Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martínez at center back. Shaw is 31, Maguire 33, Martinez 28 -- and they're all out of contract at the end of this season. Plus, a large chunk of the defensive issues can probably be directed here.

These players are all on the older side, and none of them are above-average or even average ground-covering athletes. It's really hard for a team to press without rangy defenders covering behind the press, but none of these defenders have excelled in the more passive defensive structure. Otherwise, well, United wouldn't give up so many great chances.

Pochettino seemed aware of this, as he benched Maguire for the Liverpool match and played a back three with the theoretically more mobile Leny Yoro and Matthijs De Ligt alongside Martinez. We just needed eight minutes of game time at Anfield to see that this probably isn't the solution.

Two obvious American candidates for these positions are already playing in the Premier League: Crystal Palace center back Chris Richards and Fulham left back Antonee Robinson. And there are two obvious problems with each option.

While he's used to a back three, Richards has played in much deeper defensive systems in the Premier League, and it's unclear how good Richards actually is. Futi's rating system -- which looks at how much a player increases his team's chances of scoring and decreases its chances of conceding -- sees him as a league-average player. And he's currently the senior center back on the only team with a worse defense than United.

Robinson, meanwhile, has been one of the better left backs in the Premier League over the past three or four years. Especially with Shaw's injury problems, he could provide immediate value. But while he's younger than Shaw, he's not that much younger. Robinson is 29; United don't need more 29-year-olds.

At right back, Dalot is 27, and his contract expires at the end of next season. I think he gets a bad rap; he's fine. You can win with him as a starter; you will not win if he is one of your best and most consistent starters, which has been the case at United over the past half-decade.

Alex Freeman is the standout option here. As the flex centerback/fullback that Pochettino seems to want in one of his fullback spots, Freeman was one of the breakout stars of the World Cup. He's an uber-athlete whose on-ball skill seems to improve every time he plays for the U.S., and Pochettino loves him.

As Poch said after the World Cup win over Australia: "Alex Freeman has the potential to be one of the best players in his position in the world."

At just 22, Freeman would also make Manchester United younger. He's the kind of player United need to be signing, but we also shouldn't get carried away. He has been in and out of the lineup for Villarreal this season. The betting-market-implied power ratings at PitchRank still see United as a slightly better team than Villarreal. You wouldn't be signing Freeman to make United better right now.

United got younger in the midfield this season, but the first-choice pairing of Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans is one of the least athletic in a league in which midfield play has become a rock fight combined with a 90-minute beep test. Twenty-two-year-old summer signing Andrey Santos doesn't move the needle on the physical side, and while the other 22-year-old summer signing, Carlos Baleba, does, it's still unclear whether he has the on-ball chops to hang on a team that's going to have the ball as much as United will.

Tyler Adams is playing almost every minute of every game for Bournemouth, who those market-implied ratings see as a top-15 team in the world. He's also one of the more athletic midfielders in the league. Here's how he compares to United's midfielders across a number of physical metrics from Gradient Sports. "HSR" represents "high-speed runs" or runs at a slightly lower speed than a sprint, and the outer edge of the graphic represents the 100th percentile:

The problem, of course, is that United have already invested a ton of money in midfield, and Adams turns 28 in February.

Further upfield, in attacking midfield, both Malik Tillman and Weston McKennie would add more athleticism, and they'd certainly improve United's ability to press:

Bruno Fernandes's contract is up after this season, and he's 32. If he stays, maybe the 24-year-old Tillman could come into the midfield and Bruno could bump up to the front three. Leverkusen, too, are rated ahead of United in those market-derived rankings.

But for as good as he looked at the World Cup, Tillman still hasn't locked down a consistent first-choice role since moving to the Bundesliga in summer 2025. It would be absurd to ask him to replace one of the best creative players in Premier League history. McKennie, meanwhile, is 28 years old.

Up top, we know that Folarin Balogun is available -- after the last-second failure of his previously agreed-upon move from AS Monaco to Everton over the summer. At 25, he also fits right on the edge of the age range United should be looking for. He has been productive in Ligue 1 and the Champions League whenever he has been on the field. And he would finally give United an attacker who wouldn't consistently settle for low-quality shots.

But Balogun isn't a standout presser -- he will press, but he's not adding value in that area -- and he has mostly thrived in transition-heavy attacks. United's attacking struggles have come with breaking down more set defenses. And the attack really isn't the major issue this season; only City, Brighton, Bournemouth and Liverpool have created more expected goals (xG) through 11 games.

Christian Pulisic is on fire with AC Milan, and he's good enough to play significant minutes for this United side. But they already have Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo; they don't need a third winger in his late 20s. Plus, Pulisic just signed a new, five-year deal with Milan, so his transfer fee would be especially expensive.

United are a mess, and there's at least an argument that they're in a real relegation fight right now, so they need to stop thinking about age curves and future value. They just need to bring in players who can contribute right now and make sure the unthinkable doesn't happen. And the USMNT player pool does have a bunch of players who fit that mold.

While no transfers are without risks, the likes of Richards, Adams, McKennie and Pulisic could all probably give United useful minutes as soon as they joined the club.

But those, too, are the kinds of moves that make a season like this one more likely to happen again in the future. You'd be making an already-old team even older and filling it with players who are only likely to decline.

The USMNT pool also offers tons of young talent, as we've seen with Pochettino's last few matches in charge. But that's a group of players with lots of potential. Some of them might one day be good enough to compete at the top of the Premier League, but these are mostly teenagers and guys who just entered into their 20s.

Unfortunately for Pochettino, his old team just doesn't have a lot of what his new team needs: players who can contribute today, tomorrow and a couple of years down the road.

stories.headline: Bills QB Josh Allen struggles vs. Chiefs in 'grossest' conditions
stories.summary: The Bills won their 10th game of the season Thursday vs. the Chiefs, but QB Josh Allen struggled in the weather, passing for only 81 yards.
stories.body:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- This just isn't how Bills-Chiefs games go. Especially not ones that the Bills win.

Thanksgiving 2026 belonged to the Buffalo Bills, who outlasted the Kansas City Chiefs with a 13-10 victory won on a 57-yard field goal from kicker Tyler Bass as time expired. Normally when the Bills win there are a lot more than 13 points on the scoreboard, and it's usually because quarterback Josh Allen conjured up enough dramatics, theatrics and how-did-he-do-that highlights to fill an average quarterback's season.

That Allen didn't show up Thursday. In his place was an Allen who struggled to overcome the dreary, frigid downpour, completing only 10 passes for 81 yards with two interceptions and no touchdowns. The 81 yards are the fewest Allen has passed for in any game he has started and finished. His 18.3 passer rating was the second worst in his career. It's only the fourth time Allen has won a game in which he failed to throw or run for a touchdown.

All that while facing a bitter rival against whom, historically, he has needed to play at his best. In 10 previous games against the Chiefs, counting the playoffs, Allen has accounted for 27 total touchdowns versus just four interceptions, averaged 257 passing yards and posted a passer rating of 99.7, five points better than his career mark.

"At the end of the day, we're 10-1," Allen said postgame. "It doesn't mean that we're done, that we need to stop getting better. It makes me want to play that much better. It makes me want to work that much harder. Because we are 10-1 and I feel like I still need to play better. When I feel like I can play to the best of my abilities, it'll get this offense really rolling."

For so long, a narrative has existed that the Bills go as Allen does. He's the engine, the ignition, the gas pedal and the steering wheel. But recently, that hasn't been the case. Because it wasn't just Thursday's game. Dating back to Week 3, Allen has thrown 11 interceptions versus nine touchdowns.

Meanwhile, running back James Cook is averaging 109 yards on a career-high workload over that stretch, the defense has allowed only two touchdowns in the past five games and the special teams rank top three in the league by ESPN's FPI.

For the first time in a long time, the Bills arguably aren't winning because of Josh Allen. They're just winning.

"I'm not mad if he be Superman," defensive tackle Ed Oliver said. "But I'm also not mad if he puts it on our backs, and we have to go and tighten up to make sure we get the job done. Plenty of time for the past eight years I've been seeing him put on his cape and carry this team. It's nice for a chance to say, 'Hey, relax. We've got you, man.'"

Oliver and the defense exemplified that in the final two minutes Thursday. The Bills forced a three-and-out in just 20 seconds after the two-minute warning, making the Chiefs punt from their own end zone. And when the offense couldn't capitalize, the defense forced another three-and-out in just nine seconds.

This second punt wobbled -- linebacker Joe Andreessen said he didn't get a hand on the ball but certainly "felt its wind" -- and return man Greg Dortch fielded it for a 17-yard return, setting up Bass for his game winner with four seconds left.

Everyone from Oliver to edge rusher Greg Rousseau to coach Joe Brady made sure to point out that this defensive performance came against one of the greatest passers to ever play the game, not just "another backup quarterback," as had been the criticism over the past month.

"That's an elite team over there with an elite quarterback and an elite coach, and for our guys to be like 'All right, cool,' that's what we want," Brady said. "I think it's kind of speaking to the direction that we think the guys are going, and I'm proud of them for that."

It's tough to watch that game and not imagine what this Bills defense and those Bills special teams and this vintage of Cook would all look like if paired with Allen at his best. Sure, there are excuses to be had. It started raining in Buffalo around 4 p.m. ET and hadn't let up by the time the Bills left the postgame locker room. Right tackle Spencer Brown said he picked up the ball once or twice in-game and it felt to him like a brick. Allen said these were some of the "grossest" conditions in which he has played in a decade of Buffalo home games.

If Allen knew why he was struggling, he said, he'd fix it. Brady went as far as to say there's nothing wrong with the way his quarterback is playing.

And even if that's provably untrue, that's just the confidence Brady has in his gunslinger.

"If we can win football games when our best player isn't having to be Superman," Brady said, "it's going to only pay dividends as we go because we know what Josh Allen's capable of being."

stories.headline: Jaylen Brown out against Pacers; Joel Embiid (illness) questionable
stories.summary: The 76ers' Jaylen Brown (hamstring) is out for Friday's NBA Cup game against the Pacers. Joel Embiid (illness) is questionable.
stories.body:
PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia 76ers forward Jaylen Brown (left hamstring) will miss Friday night's NBA Cup game against the Indiana Pacers.

Center Joel Embiid, who has missed the last two games with an illness, is questionable.

After scoring his sixth point of Wednesday night's win over the Miami Heat on a step-back jump shot late in the second quarter, Brown immediately shook his head and grabbed his hamstring then signaled to the Sixers bench that he needed to check out of the game. The injury started for Brown in last week's win over the Brooklyn Nets in which he tied his season high of 31 points.

Brown left that game early because of a left hamstring strain and missed the Sixers' next two wins over the Orlando Magic and Milwaukee Bucks. He returned in Monday's loss to the Portland Trail Blazers, scoring 20 points. After that game, Brown said he had "a little bit of soreness."

For the season, Brown is averaging 21.4 points, six rebounds and 3.4 assists.

Friday's game is the final of NBA Cup group play. With a win, the 76ers will clinch Eastern Conference Group B and advance to the knockout rounds for the first time.
